title: Holiness in Everyday Life
overview: God calls Israel to be holy as he is holy, and spells out what that means through a mix of worship rules and everyday fairness toward family, neighbors, the poor and foreigners.

parts.label: Be holy like God (vv. 1-8)
parts.note: The whole people, not only the priests, are called to be set apart and to reflect God's character, starting with honoring both parents, keeping the weekly day of rest and rejecting idols. A shared sacrificial meal had to be eaten within two days; the text does not say why, though one older view is that it stopped people treating leftover holy meat as magical.

parts.label: Leave some for the poor (vv. 9-10)
parts.note: Farmers were not to harvest the edges of their fields or pick up what fell or was missed, so poor people and foreigners could gather it. This built care for the needy into ordinary work, and the story of Ruth shows the custom in action.

parts.label: Fair dealing with neighbors (vv. 11-18)
parts.note: These laws target everyday wrongs such as stealing, lying, paying workers late, cursing the deaf, tripping the blind, slander and bending justice for rich or poor. Instead of hidden hatred or revenge, people are to raise a wrong openly and love their neighbor as themselves, a line Jesus later named the second greatest command.

parts.label: Mixtures and a slavery case (vv. 19-22)
parts.note: The bans on mixing animal breeds, seeds, or wool with linen are not explained; many scholars think they pictured keeping things distinct, as Israel was set apart. If a man slept with an enslaved woman promised to another man, there was to be punishment but neither was to be put to death because she was not free, and the man brought a ram as a guilt offering; scholars are unsure exactly what punishment the Hebrew word means.

parts.label: Fruit trees and banned customs (vv. 23-31)
parts.note: A new tree's fruit was left alone for three years, the fourth year's crop given to God, and only then eaten. The bans on eating blood, fortune telling, certain hair and beard cuts, gashing or marking the body for the dead, making a daughter a prostitute and consulting mediums seem mostly aimed at neighboring peoples' religious and mourning customs, though the exact meaning of some is uncertain.

parts.label: Elders, foreigners, honest scales (vv. 32-37)
parts.note: People are to stand for the elderly and treat foreigners living among them like native Israelites, loving them as themselves because Israel had once been foreigners in Egypt. The list ends with honest weights and measures in trade, tied to the God who brought them out of Egypt.

disagreement: Christians differ on how much of this chapter still applies today, with some sorting the laws into lasting moral rules and temporary ceremonial ones, and others reading the whole code as fulfilled in Jesus and summed up in the command to love.
think: Verse 34 grounds kindness to outsiders in the memory of once being outsiders; has your own experience of being on the outside shaped how you treat others?
